newsitem.title: USA: Groups look to Levitt for help on yield burning.
newsitem.headline: Groups look to Levitt for help on yield burning.

text.p: State and local government groups hope to find a valuable ally in SEC Chairman Arthur Levitt Jr when they meet with him Thursday to discuss the volatile "yield burning" issue.
The "Big Seven" state and local government groups wrote Levitt on March 18 to request a meeting because he is part of the President's influential Working Group on Financial Markets.

Groups want the working group, which has been dealing with knotty market issues since its birth after the 1987 stock market crash, to assume decisionmaking on the federal government's response to yield burning because they are deeply troubled with the Treasury Department's response to date.

"We all are sitting with a gun to our head," said Frank Shafroth, director of policy and federal relations for the National League of Cities, which took the lead in scheduling Thursday's 1430 EDT meeting between "Big Seven" state and local government groups and the Securities and Exchange Commission at SEC headquarters.
An SEC official was unavailable for comment.
In a related matter, a key U.S. House Democrat this week asked Levitt to respond to a series of questions on yield burning.

Rep. Edward Markey, D-Mass., ranking Democrat on the House Commerce Committee's subpanel on finance, wants to know what SEC is doing to coordinate yield burning activities with IRS and whether SEC "promptly" informs governments of any inquiries so that localities can address "tax consequences."

The letter asks whether SEC is keeping an eye on any National Association of Securities Dealers' probes of securities dealers concerning yield burning. And Markey asked for a list of any SEC enforcement activity on yield burning in the past five years.

Set to meet with Levitt on Thursday are Mark Schwartz, president of the Cities League; Rhode Island Treasurer Nancy Mayer on behalf of the Council of State Governments; Vernon Gray, a Howard County, Md. councilman representing the National Association of Counties; and other representatives from the National Governors' Association and National Conference of State Legislatures.

While not a member of the Big Seven, the Government Finance Officers Association also plans to send to the meeting Arthur Heilman, chairman of GFOA's governmental debt committee and director of Pennsylvania's bureau of revenue, cash flow and debt.
Yield burning refers to allegations that bond underwriters overcharge states and localities for U.S. Treasury securities purchased to help refinance outstanding bonds.
The Internal Revenue Service told municipalities last year that they can avoid having bonds declared taxable by settling any overcharges with the agency now.

But stunned muni groups told Donald Lubick, Treasury's acting assistant secretary for tax policy, at a January 27 meeting, that the vast majority of localities were unaware of any yield burning. They said that the SEC's enforcement staff, not IRS, should assume the lead on the issue by taking legal action against guilty bond underwriters.

Big Seven aides say the group has received no response from Lubick. They argue that SEC already has over 20 yield burning probes involving bond underwriters underway and that SEC action would recover losses to both the U.S. Treasury and affected states and localities.
The groups want the administration to back off of IRS' settlement offer and let the President's working group handle the issue.
A key problem, however, is that Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, who heads the working group, had to recuse himself from the issue because of his former post as co-chairman of Goldman, Sachs & Co.
Shafroth said IRS' position so far on yield burning is untenable.
"Treasury might have lost some money, but it appears that there is little question that a number of state and local governments lost money (too)," Shafroth said.

"(But) the IRS' position is you pay us whatever you were overcharged, then you go out and hire an expensive lawfirm and go to federal court and try and sue the bejesus out of those people to recover the money you lost and were mandated to pay us," Shafroth said.

Shafroth said, "Right now there is a very significant disincentive for any issuer to provide any information to the federal government" about possible yield burning in their deals "because more likely than not it would be used to hammer, instead of help, the issuer."
"So we need to discuss how to make that work," Shafroth said. "The current system isn't working."
--Vicky Stamas, 202-898-8314
